title: Mining-Induced Stress Evolution and Strata Behavior of 420 m Wide Extra-Long Fully Mechanized Longwall Face in Inner Mongolia
content: An extra-long longwall face can improve resource recovery rates, reduce roadway excavation, and minimize the frequency of working face relocation, which are crucial to sustainable and efficient production in underground coal mines. However, mining pressure is more intense in ultra-long working faces than in conventional working faces. Numerical simulations and field measurements were used to investigate mining-induced stress evolution and strata behavior at the 420 m wide extra-long fully mechanized longwall face 23301 in Inner Mongolia. Advance and lateral abutment pressure, coal pillar plastic-zone evolution, roof weighting, hydraulic support response, roadway surface displacement, and surface movement and subsidence were analyzed. The results showed that advance abutment pressure exhibited a single-peak distribution along the strike direction, with an influence range of approximately 20 m, and a three-peak distribution along the dip, with a broad flat-peak zone extending approximately 200 m in the middle of the longwall face. The lateral abutment pressure 20 m behind the coal wall reached its maximum at a mining distance of 125 m. Peak stress within the coal pillar remained approximately 1.47 m from the pillar sidewall of the haulage roadway, with a significant influence range of no more than 2.47 m. A stable load-bearing elastic zone remained within the pillar, indicating the potential to optimize the coal pillar width. Field measurements showed an average first weighting interval of the immediate roof of 18.2 m and a dynamic load factor of 1.10–1.52. The average first weighting interval and periodic weighting interval of the main roof were 47.75 and 20.02 m, respectively, with a dynamic load factor of 1.30–1.42 during periodic weighting. The surrounding rock of the haulage and return air roadways remained stable, and the thread steel bolts controlling pillar–sidewall deformation performed better than Fiber-Reinforced Polymer (FRP) bolts in the auxiliary transport roadway. Surface movement and subsidence developed around a single subsidence center, with slight uplift at several monitoring points during the initial extraction stage and a clear lag behind roof caving and strata behavior. Surface movement became essentially stable at a mining distance of 495 m, with a maximum surface subsidence of 1863 mm. These results provide practical significance for safe, efficient, and sustainable extraction of extra-long fully mechanized longwall faces.
